summary: At sunset, as the Sabbath ends, the whole town of Capernaum gathers at the door, and Jesus heals the sick and casts out demons, fulfilling Isaiah’s word.
key_insight: Mark is careful to say “when the sun had set.” The synagogue exorcism and the healing in Simon’s house had happened on the Sabbath. The town apparently waited until the Sabbath ended at sundown, when no one could object to carrying the sick or seeking healing, and then brought them all.
story: That evening, when the sun had set, {Mk} everyone who had anyone sick with various diseases brought them to Jesus, {Lk} along with many who were demon-possessed. The whole city was gathered together at the door. {Mk}
He laid His hands on every one of them and healed them. {Lk} He cast out the spirits with a word. {Mt}
Demons came out of many, crying out, “You are the Christ, the Son of God!” But He rebuked them and did not allow them to speak, for they knew that He was the Christ. {Lk}
So the word spoken by Isaiah the prophet was fulfilled: “He Himself took our infirmities And bore our sicknesses.” {Mt}
differences: Mark says “when the sun had set,” Luke “When the sun was setting,” and Matthew “When evening had come.”
Only Mark says the whole city gathered at the door. Only Luke says Jesus laid His hands on every one of them. Matthew says He cast out the spirits “with a word.”
Matthew says many were brought and He healed all; Mark says all were brought and He healed many.
Luke records what the demons cried, “You are the Christ, the Son of God!” Matthew alone quotes Isaiah 53:4.

fit.question: Mark says they brought all the sick and Jesus healed “many.” Matthew says they brought “many” and He healed “all.” Did some go home unhealed?

points.label: “Many” means a great number
points.text: In Hebrew and Aramaic speech, “many” often means a great multitude, not a part of the whole. Isaiah’s Servant bore “the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12), meaning a vast company. Mark stresses the size of the crowd; Matthew stresses that none were turned away.

points.label: Luke settles it
points.text: Luke says Jesus laid His hands “on every one of them and healed them” (Luke 4:40). Everyone who was brought that evening was healed.

fit.note: The writers describe the same evening from different angles, and Luke’s “every one” shows that Mark’s “many” never meant that some were left out.
fit.short: “Many” means a great number, not a part. Luke says Jesus healed every one of those brought to Him.

scene.label: Sundown
scene.text: The Jewish day ran from sunset to sunset, so the Sabbath ended when the sun went down. Through Jeremiah, God had forbidden carrying burdens on the Sabbath (Jeremiah 17:21–22), and seeking healing on that day was disputed; one synagogue ruler told the sick to come on the six working days instead (Luke 13:14). After sunset, no one could object.

scene.label: Isaiah 53:4
scene.text: Isaiah 53 describes the Servant of the Lord who suffers for His people. Where English versions of Isaiah read “griefs” and “sorrows,” Matthew renders the Hebrew directly as infirmities and sicknesses. Christians differ on how much bodily healing this promises before the resurrection, but Matthew plainly ties Jesus’ healing work to the Servant who bears His people’s burdens.

scene.label: Silenced demons
scene.text: The demons spoke the truth about Jesus, and He would not let them say it. He would make Himself known in His own way and time, and not by the testimony of unclean spirits.

witnesses.matthew: Quotes Isaiah 53:4 and sees the evening’s healings as fulfilled prophecy, one of several places where he links Jesus to Isaiah’s Servant (see also Matthew 12:17–21). For Matthew the healings are more than kindness; they show who Jesus is.
witnesses.mark: Gives the vivid picture of the whole town crowded at the door, and ends the day with Jesus silencing the demons “because they knew Him.” Throughout Mark, Jesus keeps His identity from being shouted abroad until the cross makes clear what kind of Messiah He is.
witnesses.luke: Notes the personal touch: He laid His hands “on every one of them.” Luke also records what the demons cried, “You are the Christ, the Son of God!”, and says Jesus silenced them because they knew He was the Christ.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the Servant who carries the weakness of His people. A whole town came with every kind of sickness and torment, and He met each one with His own hands.
seeing.living: No one in that crowd was too much for Him, and no one was handled as a number. Bring the sick and the troubled to Jesus in prayer, one by one, as Capernaum brought them to His door.
seeing.ponder: What weakness of yours, or of someone you love, do you need to bring to the One who “Himself took our infirmities”?

preaching.big_idea: The Servant who bears our sicknesses welcomes every one who is brought to Him.
outline: A word that frees and heals (16b)
A Servant who carries our burdens (17)
preaching.watch_for: Matthew draws his quotation from Isaiah 53, the chapter of the suffering Servant. The same Servant who carries sicknesses here will be “wounded for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5).
